BRIGADIER.name: Wellington
BRIGADIER.bio: Arthur Wellesley, Duke of Wellington, built his reputation in India before six years commanding the Peninsular campaign against Napoleon's marshals, mastering the reverse-slope defence and the disciplined volley line that broke French columns at Salamanca and Vitoria. Cautious by temperament and famously unsentimental about his own men, he preferred to fight on ground of his own choosing and let the enemy exhaust itself first. At Waterloo he commanded a scratch Anglo-Allied army and held the ridge at Mont-Saint-Jean through a full day of assault until the Prussians arrived. He never lost a pitched battle he commanded outright. Holds one Leadership Roll for the match, a single guaranteed Rally save for a unit under his command.

BRIGADIER.name: Thomas Graham
BRIGADIER.bio: Thomas Graham, later 1st Baron Lynedoch, took up soldiering unusually late in life after the death of his wife, joining the army in his forties and rising through the Peninsular War on sheer aptitude rather than patronage. He commanded the Anglo-Portuguese-Spanish force that won the Battle of Barrosa in 1811, a hard-fought action in which his troops captured a French Imperial Eagle. Wellington rated him among his most capable subordinates and trusted him with independent commands, including the operations around Cádiz. He retired from active field command before Waterloo but remained one of the era's most respected British generals. Holds one Leadership Roll for the match, a single guaranteed Rally save for a unit under his command.

BRIGADIER.name: Uxbridge
BRIGADIER.bio: Henry Paget, 2nd Earl of Uxbridge, commanded the Allied cavalry at Waterloo, leading the famous, costly charge of the Household and Union Brigades that shattered d'Erlon's advancing infantry columns before running out of control into the French guns. A skilled and aggressive cavalry commander with Peninsular experience, he lost a leg to one of the last cannon shots of the battle, reputedly telling Wellington 'By God, sir, I've lost my leg!' and receiving the reply 'By God, sir, so you have!'. He later served as a senior political and military figure and was created Marquess of Anglesey. Holds one Leadership Roll for the match, a single guaranteed Rally save for a unit under his command.

GUARD.name: 42nd Black Watch
GUARD.bio: The 42nd (Royal Highland) Regiment of Foot, the Black Watch, traces its roots to independent Highland companies raised in the 1720s to police the Highlands, later formed into a regiment of the line in 1739. Renowned for their dark tartan and unbending discipline, they fought with distinction throughout the Napoleonic Wars, including at Quatre Bras in 1815 where they were caught in the open by French cavalry and formed square under fire, holding despite heavy losses. Their reputation for steadiness under pressure made them one of the most trusted infantry regiments in Wellington's army. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

GUARD.name: 92nd Gordon Highlanders
GUARD.bio: Raised in 1794 by the Duke of Gordon, the 92nd Regiment of Foot became one of the most celebrated Highland regiments of the era, fighting through Egypt, the Peninsula, and the Waterloo campaign. At Quatre Bras and again at Waterloo they distinguished themselves alongside the Scots Greys, with a famous, much-embellished tradition holding that Highlanders clung to the cavalry's stirrups as they charged together into the French lines. Their kilted, tightly-drilled ranks became a symbol of Highland fighting spirit in British popular memory. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: 95th Rifles
INFANTRY.bio: Formed in 1800 as an experimental corps and issued the Baker rifle rather than the standard musket, the 95th Rifles pioneered skirmishing tactics for the British Army: fighting in loose order, picking off officers and gun crews at range, and screening the main battle line. Dressed in dark green rather than red to help them blend into cover, they became the elite reconnaissance and sharpshooting arm of Wellington's Peninsular army and fought at nearly every major action from Vimeiro to Waterloo. Their distinctive role later inspired countless popular depictions of the Napoleonic rifleman. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: Corsican Rangers
INFANTRY.bio: Formed from Corsican exiles who had fought alongside the British on their home island in the 1790s, the Royal Corsican Rangers were reconstituted in 1803 as a light infantry corps of riflemen for Mediterranean service. Filled out with recruits from Sicily, Sardinia and Naples, they fought at the Battle of Maida in 1806 and spent most of the wars campaigning around the Ionian Islands, far from the main Peninsular theatre. Their green uniforms and skirmishing role made them a natural companion to the more famous rifle regiments, though their service is much less well known. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: 44th East Essex
INFANTRY.bio: The 44th (East Essex) Regiment of Foot served through the Peninsular War and the Waterloo campaign, forming part of Picton's 5th Division alongside the Highland regiments. At Quatre Bras they held their ground against repeated French attacks in confused, close-quarters fighting through the crops and hedgerows around the crossroads. Steady, unglamorous line infantry of exactly the kind Wellington relied on to hold a position under sustained pressure, the 44th's Waterloo campaign service later earned it a battle honour still carried by its successor regiments. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: 28th North Gloucestershire
INFANTRY.bio: The 28th (North Gloucestershire) Regiment of Foot earned a unique distinction in Egypt in 1801: attacked from front and rear simultaneously at the Battle of Alexandria, the regiment's rear rank turned about to fight back-to-back with the front rank, a feat commemorated ever after by the regiment wearing its cap badge on both the front and back of its headdress. By Waterloo they were veteran Peninsular infantry serving in Picton's division, fighting at Quatre Bras and standing in the thick of the fighting near La Haye Sainte on the day of the main battle. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: 3rd Regiment of Foot Guards
INFANTRY.bio: The 3rd Regiment of Foot Guards, later the Scots Guards, served as part of the elite Guards brigades that anchored Wellington's Peninsular and Waterloo armies. At the Battle of Barrosa in 1811 under Thomas Graham, elements of the regiment took part in the assault that captured a French Imperial Eagle, one of the first taken by the British in the wars. Guards regiments were held to the highest standard of drill and discipline in the army and were routinely trusted with the most exposed or decisive ground in a battle line. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: Brunswick Oels Jägers
INFANTRY.bio: Raised in 1809 by Frederick William, Duke of Brunswick, as part of his volunteer 'Black Brunswickers' corps, the Oels Jägers wore mourning black in defiance of Napoleon's occupation of their homeland and fought their way across Germany before taking refuge in British service. They served through the Peninsular War at Fuentes de Oñoro, Salamanca and Vitoria, then returned for the Hundred Days in 1815, where the Duke himself was killed at Quatre Bras. A scratch, hard-luck unit patched together from refugees and volunteers, they nonetheless fought on to Waterloo under Wellington's command. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

HEAVY_CAV.name: Scots Greys
HEAVY_CAV.bio: The 2nd Dragoons, universally known as the Scots Greys for their distinctive grey horses, are the single most famous cavalry regiment of Waterloo. In the great charge of the Union Brigade they smashed into d'Erlon's advancing infantry columns and captured the Eagle of the French 45e Régiment de Ligne, a feat still commemorated in British military tradition. Like the rest of the Union Brigade they charged too far and were badly cut up by French cavalry and artillery on the counter-charge, but their initial impact broke the back of Napoleon's first great infantry assault. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

HEAVY_CAV.name: Royal Horse Guards – The Blues
HEAVY_CAV.bio: The Royal Horse Guards, nicknamed 'The Blues' for their distinctive blue coats among an otherwise scarlet-clad heavy cavalry, formed part of the Household Brigade at Waterloo alongside the Life Guards. They took part in the same devastating charge that broke the leading French cuirassier and infantry attacks in the early afternoon of the battle, before being thrown into repeated cavalry melees for the rest of the day. As one of the most senior and prestigious regiments in the British Army, they were entrusted with a central position near Wellington's own command post on the ridge. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

LIGHT_CAV.name: 10th Hussars
LIGHT_CAV.bio: The 10th (Prince of Wales's Own Royal) Hussars carried the personal patronage of the future King George IV, who served as their Colonel and dressed them in some of the most extravagant uniforms in the British Army. Peninsular veterans of Vitoria and the Pyrenees, they returned to service for the Waterloo campaign as part of the Allied light cavalry screen, tasked with scouting, skirmishing and covering the army's flanks rather than the shock charges of the heavies. Their reputation for dash and fashionable extravagance made them one of the most talked-about regiments of the era. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

LIGHT_CAV.name: 15th Hussars
LIGHT_CAV.bio: The 15th (King's) Hussars were among the first British cavalry regiments converted to the hussar role in the 1800s, adopting the fast, lightly-equipped style pioneered by continental light cavalry. They served with distinction throughout the Peninsular War, including a celebrated action at Sahagún in 1808 where they routed a larger French cavalry force in a dawn surprise attack. By 1815 they were experienced Peninsular veterans, well suited to the harrying, scouting and flank-guard duties expected of light cavalry in a general engagement. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

ARTILLERY.name: Royal Artillery, Battery A
ARTILLERY.bio: British artillery batteries in the Napoleonic era were organised around six guns apiece, typically a mix of 6- or 9-pounder cannon and howitzers, crewed by professional gunners of the Royal Artillery rather than regimental soldiers. At Waterloo, Wellington's guns were deployed along the ridge line and did brutal execution on the massed French infantry and cavalry columns advancing across the valley, though the batteries themselves were repeatedly overrun and retaken as the French cavalry surged past them. Gunners were trained to spike their own pieces and shelter beneath the guns rather than abandon them outright. If brigaded entirely with Cavalry, fights as Horse Artillery at Cavalry speed, except when crossing a ploughed field.

ARTILLERY.name: Royal Artillery, Battery B
ARTILLERY.bio: By 1815 the Royal Artillery had developed into one of the most professional and best-drilled arms in any European army, its gun crews capable of firing several rounds a minute of case shot at point-blank range into approaching infantry and cavalry. Batteries like this one formed the backbone of Wellington's defensive line at Waterloo, their fire credited with breaking up the momentum of both d'Erlon's infantry assault and the great French cavalry charges that followed. Horse artillery batteries could also move at the gallop to reinforce a threatened point of the line at short notice. If brigaded entirely with Cavalry, fights as Horse Artillery at Cavalry speed, except when crossing a ploughed field.

BRIGADIER.name: Napoleon
BRIGADIER.bio: Napoleon Bonaparte rose from Corsican artillery officer to Emperor of the French, reshaping European warfare with his mastery of rapid manoeuvre, concentrated artillery and the corps system that let his armies move and fight independently before combining for the decisive blow. Exiled to Elba in 1814, he returned to France in 1815 for the Hundred Days, rebuilding an army in weeks and marching north to strike the Allied and Prussian forces before they could unite. At Waterloo he commanded in person, holding the Imperial Guard back as his last reserve until it was almost too late, and his defeat there ended his rule for good. Holds one Leadership Roll for the match, a single guaranteed Rally save for a unit under his command.

BRIGADIER.name: Soult
BRIGADIER.bio: Nicolas Jean-de-Dieu Soult was one of Napoleon's most capable marshals, a veteran of Austerlitz and years of hard campaigning against Wellington in the Peninsula, where the two men developed a deep mutual respect as adversaries. At Waterloo he served as Napoleon's chief of staff, a role for which contemporaries judged him poorly suited compared to the more meticulous Berthier, and several of the army's communication failures during the battle have been laid at his door. Despite this, his record as a battlefield commander in his own right was formidable, and he later served as a French statesman. Holds one Leadership Roll for the match, a single guaranteed Rally save for a unit under his command.

BRIGADIER.name: Murat
BRIGADIER.bio: Joachim Murat, King of Naples and Napoleon's brother-in-law, was widely regarded as the finest cavalry commander of the age, famous for leading charges in person at the head of his men in flamboyant, plumed uniforms of his own design. He commanded the Grande Armée's cavalry reserve through its greatest campaigns, from Austerlitz to the retreat from Moscow, using speed and shock action to break enemy lines before the infantry arrived. He was not present at Waterloo, having been estranged from Napoleon after his own attempt to keep his throne in 1814, but his reputation as the embodiment of aggressive cavalry leadership endured. Holds one Leadership Roll for the match, a single guaranteed Rally save for a unit under his command.

GUARD.name: 1er Grenadiers à Pied
GUARD.bio: The 1er Régiment de Grenadiers à Pied de la Garde Impériale were the senior regiment of Napoleon's Old Guard, an elite corps of veteran soldiers who had to meet strict service and height requirements and were paid and equipped far better than ordinary line infantry. Held back as the army's last reserve in almost every major battle, they were thrown into the fighting only at the decisive moment, most famously in their final, doomed advance up the ridge at Waterloo in the evening of 18 June 1815. Their repulse, unprecedented in the Guard's history, was the moment the French army's morale finally broke. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

GUARD.name: 2e Grenadiers à Pied
GUARD.bio: The 2e Régiment de Grenadiers à Pied served alongside the 1er Grenadiers as part of the Old Guard's Grenadier division, an intensely proud formation that considered itself the finest infantry in Europe. Their distinctive bearskin caps and blue uniforms with white facings made them instantly recognisable, and their presence in reserve was often enough to steady a wavering French line simply by being visible on the field. Like the rest of the Guard, they were committed at Waterloo only once the battle had reached its crisis, advancing into the Allied line as dusk approached. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: 9e Légère
INFANTRY.bio: The 9e Régiment d'Infanterie Légère, light infantry trained for skirmishing and rapid manoeuvre ahead of the main battle line, served through many of Napoleon's Peninsular and German campaigns. Light infantry regiments like the 9e Légère screened the advance of the heavier line formations, harassing the enemy with sustained musketry from loose order before falling back to let the massed columns deliver the decisive blow. Voltigeur companies within regiments like this one were specifically trained as elite skirmishers, drawn from the most agile and accurate marksmen in the unit. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: 17e Légère
INFANTRY.bio: The 17e Régiment d'Infanterie Légère fought through the Napoleonic Wars as part of France's light infantry arm, prized for speed and independence of action on campaigns that increasingly relied on rapid marching and flexible deployment. Légère regiments carried a certain esprit de corps distinct from the line infantry, considering themselves the more dashing, skirmish-hardened troops of Napoleon's armies. By the time of the Hundred Days in 1815, regiments like the 17e were largely made up of hardened veterans recalled to service for one final campaign. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: 1er Ligne
INFANTRY.bio: The 1er Régiment de Ligne carried the seniority of being the first-numbered infantry regiment in Napoleon's army, a lineage stretching back through the Revolutionary Wars. Ligne regiments formed the backbone of French infantry tactics, advancing in dense columns designed to punch through an enemy line with weight and momentum rather than the extended firing lines favoured by the British. By 1815 most Ligne regiments were rebuilt around a core of Napoleonic veterans mixed with fresh conscripts hurriedly called up for the Hundred Days campaign. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: 4e Ligne
INFANTRY.bio: The 4e Régiment de Ligne served as standard French line infantry throughout the Napoleonic Wars, trained to advance in massed column formation and rely on the bayonet and sheer weight of numbers to break an enemy position. Regiments like the 4e formed the bulk of d'Erlon's I Corps at Waterloo, the great infantry assault that opened the battle's main fighting and was ultimately broken by the British infantry line and the charge of the Union and Household Brigades. Their voltigeur companies screened the advance with skirmish fire before the main column closed to contact. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: 45e Ligne
INFANTRY.bio: The 45e Régiment de Ligne holds a grim distinction in British military memory: it was this regiment's Imperial Eagle that was captured by Sergeant Charles Ewart of the Scots Greys during the Union Brigade's charge at Waterloo, one of the most celebrated trophies of the battle and still commemorated in British regimental tradition today. The loss of an Eagle was considered a catastrophic disgrace in the French army, akin to losing a regiment's soul, and the 45e's story is inseparable from that single moment of the battle. The regiment itself, like the rest of d'Erlon's Corps, was broken in the same attack that cost it its standard. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: 105e Ligne
INFANTRY.bio: The 105e Régiment de Ligne fought as line infantry in Napoleon's armies, one of many regiments whose voltigeur companies were trained as skirmishers to screen the advance of the main column. Regiments numbered this high in the French army's order of battle were often raised relatively late in the wars, reflecting the constant expansion and reorganisation Napoleon's manpower demands forced on the army. By 1815 the 105e, like its counterparts, was a mix of hardened survivors of earlier campaigns and fresh recruits swept up for the Hundred Days. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

HEAVY_CAV.name: 5e Cuirassiers
HEAVY_CAV.bio: The 5e Régiment de Cuirassiers rode as heavy shock cavalry, protected by steel breastplates and backplates that gave the cuirassiers their name and made them instantly recognisable thundering across a battlefield. At Waterloo, massed French cuirassier charges repeatedly slammed into the British infantry squares along the ridge, unable to break the disciplined formations but inflicting terror and heavy losses on the gunners caught in the open between charges. Their armour made them formidable against infantry fire and sabre cuts alike, though it could do little against a square that held its nerve and its volleys. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

HEAVY_CAV.name: Carabiniers-à-Cheval
HEAVY_CAV.bio: The Carabiniers-à-Cheval were among the most elite heavy cavalry in Napoleon's army, originally distinguished by ornate uniforms before being issued cuirasses like their cuirassier counterparts after suffering heavy losses without armour earlier in the wars. Considered a match for any cavalry in Europe, they were held as a shock reserve to be committed at the decisive moment of a battle, their charge intended to finish off an enemy line already broken by infantry and artillery. Their presence on a battlefield signalled that a commander was ready to gamble on a single, war-deciding blow. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

LIGHT_CAV.name: 7e Hussards
LIGHT_CAV.bio: The 7e Régiment de Hussards served as fast, lightly-equipped cavalry in the French light cavalry arm, tasked with scouting, screening the army's movements and harassing an enemy's flanks and supply lines rather than delivering the heavy shock charges of the cuirassiers. Hussar regiments prided themselves on dash and individual horsemanship, adopting elaborate braided uniforms inspired by Hungarian cavalry traditions. By the Hundred Days, regiments like the 7e were essential to Napoleon's ability to track Allied and Prussian troop movements across the Belgian countryside in the days before Waterloo. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

LIGHT_CAV.name: 11e Hussards
LIGHT_CAV.bio: The 11e Régiment de Hussards fought as part of Napoleon's light cavalry screen, relied upon for the unglamorous but essential work of reconnaissance, outpost duty and rapid pursuit of a beaten enemy. Hussars were expected to range far ahead of the main army, and a regiment's reputation rested as much on the reliability of the intelligence it brought back as on its performance in a charge. In the fast-moving, information-starved opening days of the Waterloo campaign, light cavalry like the 11e played a critical role in each side's attempts to work out where the other's army actually was. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

ARTILLERY.name: French Foot Artillery, Battery A
ARTILLERY.bio: Napoleon began his career as an artillery officer and never lost his conviction that guns, concentrated in mass and used aggressively, could decide a battle before the infantry ever closed. French foot artillery batteries were the tool of his signature 'grand battery' tactic: massing dozens of guns to smash a single point in the enemy line before sending infantry columns through the gap. At Waterloo, French artillery pounded the Allied ridge for hours, though the reverse-slope positions Wellington favoured sheltered many of his infantry from the worst of the bombardment. If brigaded entirely with Cavalry, fights as Horse Artillery at Cavalry speed, except when crossing a ploughed field.

ARTILLERY.name: French Foot Artillery, Battery B
ARTILLERY.bio: French gunners were widely regarded as the best-drilled artillery arm in Europe, a legacy of the technical, mathematically-minded training culture Napoleon himself had come up through as a young officer. Batteries like this one were expected to move forward aggressively to support an infantry advance, unlimbering close to the enemy line to fire canister at point-blank range, a far riskier doctrine than the more static defensive gunnery favoured by British batteries. This aggression made French artillery devastating when it worked, but exposed the guns and their crews to heavy losses when a charge or advance stalled. If brigaded entirely with Cavalry, fights as Horse Artillery at Cavalry speed, except when crossing a ploughed field.

BRIGADIER.name: Blücher
BRIGADIER.bio: Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher was past seventy when he led the Army of Silesia through the War of Liberation, a hard-riding old hussar whose men called him Marshal Forwards. At Haynau in May 1813 he sprang an ambush with some twenty squadrons of Landwehr cavalry that rode over Maison's division and restored the confidence of Prussia's raw horsemen. That August he turned on Macdonald at the Katzbach, where rain soaked the muskets and the fight was settled with cold steel. In 1815 he kept his word to Wellington, marching his battered army to Waterloo in time to strike the French right at Plancenoit. Holds one Leadership Roll for the match, a single guaranteed Rally save for a unit under his command.

BRIGADIER.name: Bülow
BRIGADIER.bio: Friedrich Wilhelm von Bülow commanded the Prussian III Corps in the Army of the North in 1813, and twice turned back French drives on Berlin. His victory at Dennewitz in September 1813 routed Ney's army and earned him the title Graf Bülow von Dennewitz. In 1815 his IV Corps led the Prussian arrival at Waterloo, fighting house by house through Plancenoit against Napoleon's Young and Old Guard. A blunt and independent commander, he was known to act first and explain himself afterwards. Holds one Leadership Roll for the match, a single guaranteed Rally save for a unit under his command.

BRIGADIER.name: Lützow
BRIGADIER.bio: Ludwig Adolf Wilhelm von Lützow served with Schill's free corps before Scharnhorst gave him permission in 1813 to raise his own: a volunteer force of infantry, cavalry and Tyrolean riflemen meant to strike the French rear and rally the smaller German states. Its students, poets and gymnasts made it the most celebrated volunteer unit of the war, immortalised in Theodor Körner's song of Lützow's wild, daring hunt. Lützow himself wore a black hussar uniform and was badly wounded twice at the head of his cavalry, the second time at the Göhrde. The black, red and gold of his corps later became the colours of Germany. Holds one Leadership Roll for the match, a single guaranteed Rally save for a unit under his command.

GUARD.name: 1st Foot Guards
GUARD.bio: Formed in 1806 from Prussia's older foot guard regiments, the Foot Guard Regiment was the senior infantry of the Prussian crown, and every Prince of Prussia was commissioned into its ranks on his tenth birthday. In the spring campaign of 1813 it fought at Grossgörschen and then at Bautzen, where it supported the Coalition positions around Bliskowitz and Preititz. During the summer armistice a second Guard regiment was raised beside it and it took the name 1st Foot Guards. Volunteers fighting in its ranks followed it through the winter campaign of 1814 into France. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

GUARD.name: 2nd Foot Guards
GUARD.bio: The 2nd Foot Guards were created on 20 June 1813, during the Truce of Pläswitz, around the Normal Infantry Battalion, the model battalion that had been attached to the Foot Guard Regiment to set the standard for the rest of the Prussian infantry. Raised to strengthen the Guard as Prussia rebuilt its army for the autumn campaign, the regiment marched with the Guard into the battles of 1813 and the advance into France in 1814. Its founding marked how far the army broken at Jena had been remade in seven years. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: 9th (Colberg) Infantry Regiment
INFANTRY.bio: The Colberg Regiment carried the memory of Prussia's one success of the disastrous war of 1806 to 1807: the defence of the Pomeranian fortress of Colberg under Gneisenau, with Schill and the citizen Nettelbeck, which held out against the French until the Peace of Tilsit. When the army was rebuilt in 1808, two regiments were raised from the garrison to honour the siege, and this one took the fortress's name. Its men fought the War of Liberation in the plain 1813 field dress of covered shakos and greatcoats rolled across the shoulder. The battle honour Colberg 1807 was later worn on the regiment's helmets. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: 8th Leib-Regiment
INFANTRY.bio: The Leib-Regiment was the second of the two regiments formed in 1808 from the defenders of Colberg, taking the honoured title of the sovereign's own regiment. Renumbered the 8th when the Guard was reorganised in the summer of 1813, it fought as Brandenburg line infantry through the War of Liberation. Its veterans were men of the one garrison that had not surrendered when the rest of Prussia fell to Napoleon. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: Lützow Free Corps Infantry
INFANTRY.bio: The infantry of the Lützow Free Corps were volunteers from across Germany, many of them university students, who joined the Royal Prussian Free Corps von Lützow after it was founded in February 1813. Equipment was scarce, so civilian clothes, old uniforms and even captured enemy coats were dyed black and finished with red facings and brass buttons, earning them the name Black Hunters. The poet Theodor Körner served in the corps and fell at Gadebusch in August 1813. Their black, red and gold became the colours of the modern German flag. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: 1st East Prussian Infantry Regiment
INFANTRY.bio: Descended from the Old Prussian Infantry Regiment No. 2, one of the oldest in the army, the 1st East Prussian Infantry Regiment drew its men from the province that set the example for all Prussia when the Landwehr was raised in 1813. Battalions of the regiment had marched into Russia in 1812 with the Prussian auxiliary corps of the Grande Armée. Reunited after Lützen, they fought at the Combat of Goldberg, where the East Prussians were briefly surrounded by French cavalry in bloody street fighting until Prussian horsemen charged and secured the field. The regiment received its formal title in October 1813. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: 2nd East Prussian Infantry Regiment
INFANTRY.bio: The 2nd East Prussian Infantry Regiment shared its recruiting grounds and its history with the 1st, and in 1812 its 1st Battalion served alongside East Prussian comrades in the auxiliary corps sent into Russia under French command. That corps, led by Yorck, broke with the French at Tauroggen in December 1812, the defection that pushed Prussia into the War of Liberation. The East Prussian battalions then fought on in Yorck's corps through the campaigns of 1813. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: Silesian Landwehr
INFANTRY.bio: The Silesian Landwehr was raised in the spring of 1813 after the King's appeal To My People, a militia of ordinary Prussians called up to fight alongside the regular army. Muskets were scarce at first, and many young Silesians were uniformed simply by sewing a yellow collar onto their blue peasant smocks. At the Katzbach in August 1813 heavy rain soaked the powder and the fight was decided with cold steel and clubbed muskets; one battalion is said to have fought with muskets whose touchholes had never been drilled. The Landwehr became part of the legend of Prussian resolve in the War of Liberation. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

HEAVY_CAV.name: Gardes du Corps
HEAVY_CAV.bio: The Regiment der Gardes du Corps was the King of Prussia's own cuirassier guard, raised in 1740 and one of the most prestigious cavalry regiments in the Prussian army. In the autumn of 1806 its officers famously sharpened their swords on the steps of the French embassy in Berlin, eager for the war that would end at Jena. Rebuilt after the defeat, it rode again in the War of Liberation, a living link to the cavalry of Frederick the Great. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

HEAVY_CAV.name: Brandenburg Cuirassiers
HEAVY_CAV.bio: The Brandenburg Cuirassiers were formed in 1807 as Prussia began rebuilding its heavy cavalry after the collapse at Jena and Auerstedt. Mounted on heavy horses, they fought through the War of the Sixth Coalition in 1813 and 1814, part of the new army that drove Napoleon out of Germany. The regiment would serve Prussia for more than a century before it was finally disbanded in 1919. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

LIGHT_CAV.name: 1st Leib-Hussars
LIGHT_CAV.bio: The 1st Leib-Hussars descended from the Prittwitz Hussars, who had worn the Totenkopf, the death's head badge, since the days of Frederick the Great and still wore it at Jena in 1806. After that defeat the regiment was split in 1808 into the 1st and 2nd Leib-Hussars, both keeping the skull as their emblem. On campaign the badge was painted onto the shako cover. They became some of the most recognisable light horsemen of the War of Liberation. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

LIGHT_CAV.name: Lützow Free Corps Uhlans
LIGHT_CAV.bio: The mounted arm of the Lützow Free Corps combined uhlans, hussars and mounted jägers, the uhlans riding with red and black pennons on their lances. Raiding behind French lines during the armistice of 1813, the corps was cornered by Confederation of the Rhine troops and almost wiped out, yet its reputation was such that volunteers soon brought it back to full strength. Lützow led his horsemen in person and was wounded at their head at the Göhrde. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

ARTILLERY.name: Army of Silesia Foot Battery
ARTILLERY.bio: The foot batteries of Blücher's Army of Silesia belonged to an artillery arm rebuilt almost from nothing after the losses of 1806, and they served through the whole War of Liberation. At the Katzbach in August 1813 the storm left the infantry unable to fire, giving free rein to the Allied guns and cavalry as Macdonald's army was driven back into the flooded river. The victory gave rise to the German saying for anyone charging forward hard: he goes in like Blücher at the Katzbach. If brigaded entirely with Cavalry, fights as Horse Artillery at Cavalry speed, except when crossing a ploughed field.

ARTILLERY.name: Lützow Free Corps Battery
ARTILLERY.bio: Lützow's Free Corps was an army in miniature, with a full regiment of infantry, a mixed regiment of light cavalry and its own battery of nine guns. Like the rest of the corps its gunners went into action dressed in black, and no part of the corps carried standards. The battery supported the volunteers through the raids and the more regular fighting of 1813 in northern Germany. If brigaded entirely with Cavalry, fights as Horse Artillery at Cavalry speed, except when crossing a ploughed field.

BRIGADIER.name: Kutuzov
BRIGADIER.bio: Mikhail Kutuzov, one-eyed veteran of the Turkish wars and the defeat at Austerlitz, was given supreme command in August 1812 as Napoleon drove on Moscow. He chose to stand at Borodino, the bloodiest single day of the Napoleonic Wars, and then gave up Moscow rather than risk the army that would destroy the Grande Armée on its retreat. Patient and wily, he preferred to let hunger, winter and the Cossacks do his fighting for him. Holds one Leadership Roll for the match, a single guaranteed Rally save for a unit under his command.

BRIGADIER.name: Bagration
BRIGADIER.bio: Prince Pyotr Bagration, a Georgian-born pupil of Suvorov, commanded the Second Western Army in 1812 and was the most aggressive fighting general in Russian service. At Borodino his men held the earthworks named after him, the Bagration flèches, which French and Russians stormed eight times in the course of the day. He was mortally wounded there, and officers of the Guard saluted him as he was carried from the field. Holds one Leadership Roll for the match, a single guaranteed Rally save for a unit under his command.

BRIGADIER.name: Platov
BRIGADIER.bio: Matvei Platov, Ataman of the Don Cossacks, led Russia's irregular horse through the campaigns of 1812 to 1814. At Borodino he and Uvarov took some 12,000 Cossacks and regular cavalry across the Kalatsha to strike the French left, forcing Napoleon to postpone his great assault on the central redoubt. In the retreat that followed, his Cossacks harried the Grande Armée without rest all the way to the Niemen. Holds one Leadership Roll for the match, a single guaranteed Rally save for a unit under his command.

GUARD.name: Preobrazhensky Life Guard Regiment
GUARD.bio: The Preobrazhensky Regiment grew out of the toy army of the young Peter the Great and was formed in 1690, making it the senior regiment of the Russian Guard. In 1700 it and the Semenovsky became the first regiments to carry the title of Life Guards. At Borodino its battalions stood in reserve under artillery fire, the last uncommitted infantry of the Russian centre. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

GUARD.name: Semenovsky Life Guard Regiment
GUARD.bio: The Semenovsky Regiment, named after the village near Moscow where it was first stationed, was the second of Peter the Great's original Guard regiments. For their stand against the Swedes its men wore red stockings for forty years, because, it was said, they had stood knee-deep in blood. At Borodino it was held in reserve until the French took the Raevsky battery, then fought the French heavy cavalry in the centre of the Russian line. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: Kiev Grenadier Regiment
INFANTRY.bio: The Kiev Grenadiers served in the 2nd Grenadier Division of Bagration's Second Western Army in 1812, part of the Moscow-based grenadier formations that were the backbone of Russia's line infantry. At Borodino the division built and held the right-hand work of the Bagration flèches under repeated French assault. Like so many Russian regiments that day, the grenadiers died where they stood rather than yield ground. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: Moscow Grenadier Regiment
INFANTRY.bio: The Moscow Grenadiers fought beside the Kiev Grenadiers in the 2nd Grenadier Division, under the Prince of Mecklenburg, during the 1812 campaign. At Borodino they held the ground around the flèches and the burning village of Semenovskoye as Davout's and Ney's batteries pounded the Russian left. The division was all but destroyed in the fighting, yet the line did not break. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: Astrakhan Grenadier Regiment
INFANTRY.bio: The Astrakhan Grenadiers formed part of the 2nd Brigade of the 2nd Grenadier Division in 1812, brigaded with the Fanagoria Grenadiers. At Borodino they moved up through the shattered village of Semenovskoye to meet the French attacks on the Russian left. They fought on there under massed artillery fire and repeated charges of French cuirassiers. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: Fanagoria Grenadier Regiment
INFANTRY.bio: The Fanagoria Grenadiers carried one of the proudest traditions in the Russian army, having been shaped by Suvorov himself in the wars of the late eighteenth century. In 1812 they served in the 2nd Grenadier Division alongside the Astrakhan Grenadiers. At Borodino the regiment fought in the struggle for the flèches, among the most contested ground of the whole battle. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: Kremenchug Infantry Regiment
INFANTRY.bio: The Kremenchug Infantry Regiment marched in Baggovut's 2nd Corps of the First Western Army in 1812, brigaded with the Minsk Regiment. Ordinary musketeers rather than grenadiers, they were the steady line infantry on whom the Russian army's famous stubbornness in defence depended. At Borodino Baggovut's corps was shifted from the right wing to shore up the hard-pressed Russian left. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: Minsk Infantry Regiment
INFANTRY.bio: The Minsk Infantry Regiment served alongside the Kremenchug Regiment in Baggovut's 2nd Corps during the 1812 campaign. Recruited from the conscript peasantry that made up the bulk of the Tsar's army, its men were known across Europe for holding ground long after other troops would have broken. They fought through Borodino and the long pursuit of the Grande Armée that followed. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

HEAVY_CAV.name: Chevalier Guard Regiment
HEAVY_CAV.bio: The Chevalier Guard was the senior heavy cavalry of the Russian Guard, recruited from the nobility to protect the Tsar. At Austerlitz in 1805 it met Napoleon's Guard cavalry in a great melee and was broken by Rapp's chasseurs and Mamelukes, who captured its commander, Prince Repnin. Rebuilt, it stood behind Semenovskoye at Borodino and rode with the Guard cavalry into Paris in 1814. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

HEAVY_CAV.name: Life Guard Horse Regiment
HEAVY_CAV.bio: The Life Guard Horse Regiment was the second heavy regiment of the Russian Guard cavalry, brigaded with the Chevalier Guard. At Borodino the two regiments waited behind the houses of Semenovskoye as the French cavalry assaults crashed against the Russian centre and left. It went on to fight through the campaigns of 1813 and 1814 with the rest of the Guard. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

LIGHT_CAV.name: Akhtyrka Hussar Regiment
LIGHT_CAV.bio: The Akhtyrka Hussars are forever linked to Denis Davydov, the hussar poet who joined them as a lieutenant colonel in April 1812. Days before Borodino, near the estate where he had grown up, Davydov persuaded Bagration to let him lead a partisan detachment behind French lines, and his raids became a model for the people's war against the invader. He later commanded the regiment in France in 1814, fighting at Brienne, La Rothière, Laon and Paris. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

LIGHT_CAV.name: Don Cossacks
LIGHT_CAV.bio: The Don Cossacks were Russia's irregular light horse, raised from the free warrior communities of the southern steppe and led in 1812 by their Ataman, Platov. Too loose to fight a set battle like regular cavalry, they excelled at raids, ambushes and the endless harassment of an army on the march. During the retreat from Moscow they picked off stragglers, foragers and supply trains until the Grande Armée was a ruin. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

ARTILLERY.name: 26th Battery Company
ARTILLERY.bio: The 26th Battery Company was the heavy artillery of Raevsky's corps at Borodino, sited on the great mound in the centre of the Russian line. Raevsky fortified the position into a redoubt, and twelve of its guns, with six from the 47th Light Company, fired canister into French columns that came on regardless. The Raevsky Redoubt changed hands in some of the fiercest fighting of the war before it finally fell. If brigaded entirely with Cavalry, fights as Horse Artillery at Cavalry speed, except when crossing a ploughed field.

ARTILLERY.name: 11th Battery Company
ARTILLERY.bio: The 11th Battery Company was one of two heavy batteries that occupied the Bagration flèches at Borodino, earthworks built so that Russian guns could rake the French flank as well as their front. It held the position through the repeated assaults that made the flèches the most fought-over ground of the battle. Russia's artillery that day had many more heavy twelve-pounders than the French. If brigaded entirely with Cavalry, fights as Horse Artillery at Cavalry speed, except when crossing a ploughed field.

BRIGADIER.name: Barclay de Tolly
BRIGADIER.bio: Michael Andreas Barclay de Tolly, a Baltic German of Scottish descent, commanded the First Western Army in 1812 and devised the long retreat that drew Napoleon deep into Russia. Reviled for it at the time, he fought with great courage at Borodino, where he twice narrowly escaped death in the cavalry fighting. Restored to high command in 1813, he led the Russian forces through Leipzig and into France, and was made a field marshal after the fall of Paris. Holds one Leadership Roll for the match, a single guaranteed Rally save for a unit under his command.

BRIGADIER.name: Ostermann-Tolstoy
BRIGADIER.bio: Alexander Ostermann-Tolstoy commanded the Russian IV Corps in 1812, and at Borodino Kutuzov brought his whole corps across from the right wing to plug the gap between the Raevsky Redoubt and Semenovskoye. His men endured a devastating artillery barrage there without breaking. In 1813 he held the Guard against Vandamme's corps at Kulm, losing an arm in a stand that helped turn the autumn campaign. Holds one Leadership Roll for the match, a single guaranteed Rally save for a unit under his command.

BRIGADIER.name: Uvarov
BRIGADIER.bio: Fyodor Uvarov was a cavalry general who had risen through the Guard horse, commanding the I Cavalry Corps in 1812. At Borodino he and Platov led some 12,000 regular cavalry and Cossacks across the Kalatsha in a raid on the French left that forced Napoleon to delay his main assault on the central redoubt. He served as a close adviser to Tsar Alexander through the campaigns that followed. Holds one Leadership Roll for the match, a single guaranteed Rally save for a unit under his command.

GUARD.name: Izmailovsky Life Guard Regiment
GUARD.bio: The Izmailovsky Regiment was third in seniority of the Russian Guard infantry, after the Preobrazhensky and Semenovsky. At Borodino it stood beside Semenovskoye with the Lithuania Guard, forced to stay in square against masses of French cavalry while the French batteries across the stream tore into its ranks. Borodino was the day the Russian Guard came of age as elite troops whose commitment could turn a battle. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

GUARD.name: Lithuania Life Guard Regiment
GUARD.bio: The Lithuania (Litovsky) Life Guard Regiment was brigaded with the Izmailovsky in Ostermann-Tolstoy's command in 1812. At Borodino the two regiments held their squares near Semenovskoye for hours under cavalry charges and close-range artillery, which at times fired canister straight into the Guard's ranks. Their endurance there became one of the legends of the battle. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: Pavlov Grenadier Regiment
INFANTRY.bio: The Pavlov Grenadiers served in Stroganov's 1st Grenadier Division in 1812, brigaded with the Ekaterinoslav Grenadiers. The regiment was famous for keeping the tall brass mitre caps of an earlier age, an honour won for their conduct at Friedland in 1807, and they wore them into battle long after the rest of the army had changed. They fought at Borodino and through the campaigns that carried the Russian army to Paris. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: Ekaterinoslav Grenadier Regiment
INFANTRY.bio: The Ekaterinoslav Grenadiers marched with the Pavlov Grenadiers in the 1st Grenadier Division under Stroganov in 1812. Raised from picked men, the grenadier regiments were the heavy infantry of the Tsar's army, sent where the fighting was hardest. They fought at Borodino and in the long campaigns that followed across Germany and into France. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: Kexholm Grenadier Regiment
INFANTRY.bio: The Kexholm Regiment served in the 1st Grenadier Division, formed in 1811 when the Russian army gathered its grenadier regiments into dedicated divisions. It fought through the campaigns of 1812 to 1814, from the defence of Russia to the march on Paris. In the reorganisation of 1814 it passed to the newly formed 3rd Grenadier Division. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: Pernov Grenadier Regiment
INFANTRY.bio: The Pernov Regiment, named after the Baltic port of Pernau, served alongside the Kexholm Regiment in the 1st Grenadier Division during the wars against Napoleon. It fought through the campaigns from 1812 to the fall of Paris. In April 1814 the two regiments were transferred together to the new 3rd Grenadier Division. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: Moscow Opolchenie
INFANTRY.bio: The Moscow Opolchenie was a militia raised in 1812 from the serfs and townsmen of the Moscow region as Napoleon advanced on the old capital. Poorly armed and barely trained, its men dug many of the earthworks at Borodino, and their appearance on the Russian left gave Poniatowski's Poles cause to halt their advance. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: Life Grenadier Regiment
INFANTRY.bio: The Life Grenadier Regiment served in the 1st Grenadier Division under Stroganov in 1812, brigaded with the Arakcheyev Grenadiers. Its title marked it out as a regiment of particular honour among the army's grenadiers. It fought at Borodino and through the foreign campaigns of 1813 and 1814. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

HEAVY_CAV.name: Ekaterinoslav Cuirassier Regiment
HEAVY_CAV.bio: The Ekaterinoslav Cuirassiers rode in Knorring's 2nd Cuirassier Division at Borodino, part of Bagration's wing on the Russian left. Russia had restored the breastplate to its heavy cavalry just before the 1812 campaign, and the cuirassiers were thrown in again and again against the French horse and infantry storming the flèches and Semenovskoye. The regiment fought on through the campaigns of 1813 and 1814. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

HEAVY_CAV.name: Military Order Cuirassier Regiment
HEAVY_CAV.bio: The Military Order Cuirassiers took their name from the Order of St George, Russia's highest military decoration, and were brigaded with the Ekaterinoslav Cuirassiers in Knorring's division in 1812. At Borodino they counter-charged the French cavalry that swept into the Russian line around Semenovskoye. They went on to fight through Germany and France. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

LIGHT_CAV.name: 1st Bashkir Regiment
LIGHT_CAV.bio: The 1st Bashkir Regiment came from the southern Urals, horsemen armed with lance, whip, sword and the bow, which earned them the French nickname the Cupids of the North. In November 1813, under Benckendorff, they were among the first troops to reach Amsterdam and The Hague, and built a bridge of boats across the IJssel that served the advance for two months. They rode on with the Allied armies all the way to Paris. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

LIGHT_CAV.name: Life Guard Hussar Regiment
LIGHT_CAV.bio: The Life Guard Hussars were the light cavalry of the Russian Guard, a regiment whose officers included the young Denis Davydov before he left to make his name with the Akhtyrka Hussars. They rode with the Guard cavalry through the campaigns of 1812 to 1814 and appear in paintings of Russian Guard officers in the German and French cities of the foreign campaigns. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

ARTILLERY.name: 32nd Battery Company
ARTILLERY.bio: The 32nd Battery Company was the second of the two heavy batteries placed in the Bagration flèches at Borodino. Pierced to let each battery's twelve guns fire on the attackers, the flèches were stormed eight times by the two sides. The battery fought through one of the most savage artillery duels of the war. If brigaded entirely with Cavalry, fights as Horse Artillery at Cavalry speed, except when crossing a ploughed field.

ARTILLERY.name: Guard Artillery Brigade
ARTILLERY.bio: The Guard Artillery supported the Russian Guard infantry at Borodino, moving forward with the regiments around Semenovskoye. There it was smothered by the more numerous French guns and suffered very heavy casualties, its gunners standing to their pieces at murderous range. It went on to serve with the Guard through the campaigns of 1813 and 1814. If brigaded entirely with Cavalry, fights as Horse Artillery at Cavalry speed, except when crossing a ploughed field.

BRIGADIER.name: Archduke Charles
BRIGADIER.bio: Archduke Charles, brother of the Emperor Francis, was Austria's finest general and the reformer who rebuilt its army after the disasters of 1805. At Aspern-Essling in May 1809 he inflicted on Napoleon the first defeat the Emperor had suffered in person in a major battle. When French cavalry broke through his centre, he brought up the grenadier reserve and, by tradition, seized a colour of the Zach Regiment and led it forward himself to restore the line. Holds one Leadership Roll for the match, a single guaranteed Rally save for a unit under his command.

BRIGADIER.name: Schwarzenberg
BRIGADIER.bio: Karl Philipp, Prince Schwarzenberg, was a cavalryman who made his name with a victorious cuirassier charge at Le Cateau in 1794. In 1812 he commanded the Austrian contingent in the invasion of Russia at Napoleon's own request; a year later, with Austria at war with France, he was made commander-in-chief of the Allied armies. At Leipzig in October 1813 he directed the Battle of the Nations that broke Napoleon's power in Germany, and is said to have led a cavalry charge against Murat in person. Holds one Leadership Roll for the match, a single guaranteed Rally save for a unit under his command.

BRIGADIER.name: Liechtenstein
BRIGADIER.bio: Prince Johann of Liechtenstein was Austria's great cavalry commander, leading the reserve cavalry through the campaigns of 1805 and 1809. At Aspern, when French horsemen burst through the Austrian centre, his dragoons and cuirassiers came galloping up behind the grenadiers to drive them back. After Wagram he succeeded Archduke Charles in command of the army and negotiated the peace that followed. Holds one Leadership Roll for the match, a single guaranteed Rally save for a unit under his command.

GUARD.name: Murray Grenadier Brigade
GUARD.bio: Austria had no Imperial Guard of the French kind; its elite infantry were the grenadier battalions, formed from the grenadier companies of the line regiments and massed into a reserve under the army commander. At Aspern in 1809 Murray's brigade belonged to Lindenau's Grenadier Reserve Division. When the French cavalry broke the Austrian centre on the second day, the grenadiers were brought up at the double and formed a chequerboard of squares that stopped the charge. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

GUARD.name: Scovaud Grenadier Brigade
GUARD.bio: Scovaud's brigade was another of the four brigades of the Grenadier Reserve at Aspern, picked men in tall bearskin caps drawn from the best soldiers of Austria's German and Hungarian regiments. Held back by Archduke Charles for the decisive moment, the grenadiers were committed to plug the gap in the centre and then to the counter-attacks that drove the French back towards the Danube. Austria's grenadiers fought again as a reserve corps at Leipzig in 1813. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: IR 15 Zach
INFANTRY.bio: Infantry Regiment Nr. 15, named after its colonel-proprietor General Zach, fought at Aspern in 1809 in the corps that held the Austrian centre. It was a colour of this regiment that Archduke Charles is said to have taken in his own hand to rally the wavering line when French cavalry broke through, one of the most celebrated images of the battle. Like all Austrian line regiments it wore white coats, with its own facing colour to tell it apart. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: IR 4 Hoch- und Deutschmeister
INFANTRY.bio: Infantry Regiment Nr. 4, the Hoch- und Deutschmeister, was Vienna's own regiment, its proprietor the Grand Master of the Teutonic Order and its recruits drawn from the capital. It fought through every war against Revolutionary and Napoleonic France and became a symbol of the city it was raised in. The regiment's march remains one of the best known in Austria. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: IR 33 Hungarian
INFANTRY.bio: Infantry Regiment Nr. 33 was one of the Hungarian line regiments that made up a large part of the Austrian army, distinguished by their tight blue trousers worn with the white coat. Hungarian regiments fought at Aspern, where Hohenzollern's corps broke through the French right-centre and helped carry the battle. Hardy and aggressive, the Hungarian infantry were among the best foot soldiers of the Habsburg monarchy. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: Vienna Volunteers
INFANTRY.bio: The Vienna Volunteers were raised in 1809, when Austria called its people to arms against Napoleon in a spirit of national war new to the Habsburg monarchy. Alongside the new Landwehr militia, these battalions of citizens and students marched out to fight beside the regulars. A battalion of Vienna Volunteers fought at Aspern in May 1809. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: St. Georger Grenzers
INFANTRY.bio: The St. Georger Grenz Infantry came from the Military Frontier, the long borderland with the Ottoman Empire where every family owed military service in return for land. Grenzers were born skirmishers and hardy soldiers, used to fighting in broken ground and serving as Austria's light infantry. St. Georger Grenzers fought at Aspern in 1809. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: 2nd Jäger Battalion
INFANTRY.bio: The Jäger battalions were Austria's riflemen, recruited from huntsmen and foresters of the Alpine and Bohemian lands and armed with rifles rather than muskets. Dressed in pike grey with green facings and a round hat, they fought in open order ahead of the line, picking off officers at range. The 2nd Jäger fought at Aspern in 1809. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

HEAVY_CAV.name: Kaiser Cuirassiers
HEAVY_CAV.bio: The Kaiser Cuirassiers took the Emperor himself as proprietor and were the senior of Austria's heavy cavalry regiments. Austrian cuirassiers wore a breastplate only, without a backplate, over a white coat, and were among the best heavy horsemen in Europe. At Leipzig in 1813 Austria massed its cuirassiers into a corps under Count Nostitz, which rode into action on the southern front of the Battle of the Nations. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

HEAVY_CAV.name: Knesevich Dragoons
HEAVY_CAV.bio: The Knesevich Dragoon Regiment served at Aspern in 1809 in Clary's brigade, one of the heavy dragoon regiments of the Austrian reserve cavalry. Austrian dragoons were battle cavalry rather than mounted infantry, charging alongside the cuirassiers on big horses. In the crisis of the battle, Liechtenstein's dragoons came up behind the grenadier squares and drove off the French horsemen who had broken through the centre. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

LIGHT_CAV.name: Schwarzenberg Uhlans
LIGHT_CAV.bio: The Schwarzenberg Uhlans were the lancer regiment granted to Prince Schwarzenberg as its proprietor in reward for his service commanding Archduke Charles's rearguard. Austrian uhlans were recruited largely from Galicia, Austria's share of partitioned Poland, and carried the lance and the czapka in the Polish style. The regiment served through the wars of 1809 and 1813 to 1814 as its proprietor rose to command all the Allied armies. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

LIGHT_CAV.name: Szekler Hussars
LIGHT_CAV.bio: The Szekler Hussars were raised from the Szekler people of eastern Transylvania, a frontier community with a long tradition of mounted service. Like all Austrian hussars they were light horsemen in the Hungarian style, with braided dolman, pelisse and shako, used for scouting, raiding and pursuit. Hungary's hussars gave the whole of Europe its idea of what light cavalry should look like. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

ARTILLERY.name: Austrian Position Battery
ARTILLERY.bio: The position batteries were the heavy artillery of the Austrian army, armed with twelve-pounders and held in reserve to be massed where the fighting was hardest. At Aspern Archduke Charles brought 288 guns into action, and great batteries filled the open ground between the villages of Aspern and Essling. Their fire tore into the French columns crossing the Marchfeld. If brigaded entirely with Cavalry, fights as Horse Artillery at Cavalry speed, except when crossing a ploughed field.

ARTILLERY.name: Austrian Cavalry Battery
ARTILLERY.bio: The Austrian cavalry batteries supported the mounted arm with light guns, their gunners riding on the gun carriages and a padded ammunition wagon known as the sausage rather than on horses of their own. The arrangement kept the batteries cheap and fast enough to follow the cavalry into action. They served with the reserve cavalry from 1805 through to the campaigns of 1813 and 1814. If brigaded entirely with Cavalry, fights as Horse Artillery at Cavalry speed, except when crossing a ploughed field.

BRIGADIER.name: Castaños
BRIGADIER.bio: Francisco Javier Castaños commanded the Spanish Army of Andalusia in the summer of 1808, when Spain rose against Napoleon's attempt to put his brother Joseph on its throne. At Bailén in July his army surrounded General Dupont's corps and forced it to surrender, the first time a French army in the field had laid down its arms to an enemy. The victory shocked Europe and showed that the Emperor's armies could be beaten. Holds one Leadership Roll for the match, a single guaranteed Rally save for a unit under his command.

BRIGADIER.name: Palafox
BRIGADIER.bio: José de Palafox was the young captain-general who led the defence of Zaragoza through its two great sieges of 1808 and 1809. With a garrison of regulars, volunteers and armed townspeople he fought the French street by street and house by house, refusing every summons to surrender. Zaragoza fell only in February 1809, after disease and bombardment had killed much of the city, and its defence became a symbol of Spanish resistance. Holds one Leadership Roll for the match, a single guaranteed Rally save for a unit under his command.

BRIGADIER.name: La Serna
BRIGADIER.bio: José de la Serna joined the defence of Zaragoza in 1808 as a lieutenant colonel and commanded batteries during the second siege, wearing the defenders' medal for the rest of his life as his favourite distinction. Captured when the city fell, he soon escaped. Sent to South America in 1816, he became the last Viceroy of Peru in 1821, and fought his final battle at Ayacucho in December 1824, where he was wounded and captured as the patriot army of Sucre sealed the independence of Peru. Holds one Leadership Roll for the match, a single guaranteed Rally save for a unit under his command.

GUARD.name: Reales Guardias Españolas
GUARD.bio: The Royal Spanish Guards were the senior infantry regiment of the Spanish Royal Household, the foot guard of the Bourbon kings since the early eighteenth century. When Napoleon seized the Spanish royal family in 1808, the Guards were among the regular troops who joined the national rising. They fought through the Peninsular War as the elite of Spain's regular infantry. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

GUARD.name: Guardias Valonas
GUARD.bio: The Walloon Guards were the second regiment of the Spanish Royal Guard infantry, originally raised in the Spanish Netherlands and long recruited from Walloons and other Catholic foreigners. They fought against the French throughout the Peninsular War. Among the young officers who began their careers in the regiment was José de Canterac, who later served as La Serna's chief of staff in Peru and signed the capitulation after Ayacucho in 1824. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: Voluntarios de Aragón
INFANTRY.bio: The Volunteers of Aragon were raised by Palafox in 1808 from the men of Zaragoza and the surrounding countryside when the city rose against the French. Half-trained and poorly equipped, they fought in the defence of their own streets and convents through both sieges, alongside regulars, priests and townspeople. Among the officers who fought at Zaragoza was José de la Mar, who would later become President of Peru. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: Regimiento de Sevilla
INFANTRY.bio: The Seville Regiment was one of the long-established line regiments of the Spanish army, recruited from Andalusia. In 1808 the Andalusian regulars formed the core of Castaños's army, the force that won Spain's greatest victory of the war at Bailén. Spanish line infantry wore white coats with regimental facings, much like the old Bourbon armies of the eighteenth century. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: Regimiento de Zamora
INFANTRY.bio: The Zamora Regiment was a Spanish line regiment of the old royal army, which went into the war of 1808 with a long history behind it. Spain's regular regiments bore the brunt of the war's pitched battles, often outnumbered and poorly supplied, while the guerrillas harried the French behind the lines. The regiment fought on through the long years of the Peninsular War. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: Regimiento de Soria
INFANTRY.bio: The Soria Regiment was one of the old line regiments of the Spanish army, its traditions stretching back to the tercios of the sixteenth century. In the Peninsular War Spain's line regiments were repeatedly broken and rebuilt, but kept returning to the field year after year. Their persistence tied down hundreds of thousands of French troops that Napoleon badly needed elsewhere. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: Regimiento de Irlanda
INFANTRY.bio: The Irlanda Regiment was one of Spain's Irish regiments, raised from Irish exiles who had served the Spanish crown since the seventeenth century, and still officered by men of Irish descent in 1808. With the Hibernia and Ultonia regiments it carried on the tradition of the Wild Geese in Spanish service. In the Peninsular War it fought for Spain against the French. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: Regimiento de Cataluña
INFANTRY.bio: The Catalonia Regiment was a Spanish line regiment from the principality where some of the war's longest and most bitter fighting took place. In Catalonia regular troops, the local miquelets and somatén militias fought the French in sieges and mountain warfare from 1808 until the end of the war. Many of the Empire's Italian and German troops were sent there to fight them. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

HEAVY_CAV.name: Carabineros Reales
HEAVY_CAV.bio: The Royal Carabiniers were the heavy cavalry of the Spanish Royal Household, the senior mounted regiment of the Bourbon army. Mounted on big Andalusian horses, they fought as battle cavalry through the Peninsular War. Spain's cavalry suffered badly for want of horses after the first campaigns, making regiments like the Carabiniers precious. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

HEAVY_CAV.name: Regimiento de Borbón
HEAVY_CAV.bio: The Borbón Regiment was a Spanish cavalry regiment that fought in the campaign of Bailén in 1808. Among its officers was a young captain, José de San Martín, promoted for his conduct at Arjonilla shortly before the battle. San Martín later sailed for South America, crossed the Andes to free Chile, and in 1821 proclaimed the independence of Peru and became its Protector. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

LIGHT_CAV.name: Húsares de María Luisa
LIGHT_CAV.bio: The María Luisa Hussars, named after the Queen of Spain, were one of the hussar regiments of the regular Spanish army. Like hussars everywhere they wore braided dolmans and pelisses and served as scouts, raiders and skirmishers. In the long war against the French they fought alongside the guerrilla bands that made every road in Spain dangerous for an enemy courier. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

LIGHT_CAV.name: Cazadores de Olivenza
LIGHT_CAV.bio: The Olivenza Chasseurs were one of Spain's regular light cavalry regiments, named after the frontier town of Olivenza that Spain had taken from Portugal in 1801. Mounted light horsemen trained for scouting and outpost work, they served through the Peninsular War. Spain's light cavalry often fought in small detachments supporting the regular armies and the guerrillas. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

ARTILLERY.name: Battery of Bailén
ARTILLERY.bio: The Spanish Royal Artillery Corps was a professional, well-trained arm, and its guns played a vital part in the victory at Bailén in July 1808. In the summer heat the Spanish artillery outgunned Dupont's batteries as the French tried to break out of the trap Castaños had closed around them. Dupont's surrender was the first capitulation of a French army in the field. If brigaded entirely with Cavalry, fights as Horse Artillery at Cavalry speed, except when crossing a ploughed field.

ARTILLERY.name: Battery of Cádiz
ARTILLERY.bio: The guns of Cádiz held the city through the great French siege from 1810 to 1812, when the port became the seat of Spain's free government and its parliament wrote the liberal Constitution of 1812. Protected by the sea and supplied by the Royal Navy, the defenders never let the French close in. Spanish gunners manned the city's batteries throughout the siege. If brigaded entirely with Cavalry, fights as Horse Artillery at Cavalry speed, except when crossing a ploughed field.

BRIGADIER.name: Beresford
BRIGADIER.bio: William Carr Beresford was the British general given command of the Portuguese army in 1809, with the rank of Marshal. In a few years he turned a demoralised force into one that Wellington trusted to stand in line beside his own regiments, retraining its officers, restoring its discipline and brigading Portuguese regiments into British divisions. In 1811 he commanded the Allied army at the bloody battle of Albuera. Holds one Leadership Roll for the match, a single guaranteed Rally save for a unit under his command.

BRIGADIER.name: Lecor
BRIGADIER.bio: Carlos Frederico Lecor commanded Portuguese brigades and divisions through the Peninsular War, rising to lead the 7th Division of Wellington's army in the final campaigns. In 1815 he was given command of the Royal Volunteers of the Prince, a division of Peninsular veterans sent to serve in Brazil. He conquered the Banda Oriental and took Montevideo in 1817, and after Brazil's independence he served the new Empire, ending his days in Rio de Janeiro as a Marshal of the Brazilian Army and Viscount of Laguna. Holds one Leadership Roll for the match, a single guaranteed Rally save for a unit under his command.

BRIGADIER.name: Silveira
BRIGADIER.bio: Francisco da Silveira, later Count of Amarante, was a Portuguese general who led the resistance in the north of the country when Marshal Soult invaded in 1809. Commanding a mixture of regulars and militia, he fought the French at the bridge of Amarante and cut their communications as Soult fell back from Porto. He became one of Portugal's national heroes of the war. Holds one Leadership Roll for the match, a single guaranteed Rally save for a unit under his command.

GUARD.name: 2nd Caçadores
GUARD.bio: The Caçadores, Portugal's light infantry hunters, were the elite of Beresford's reformed army, dressed in brown and trained as skirmishers to work alongside the British Light Division and riflemen. The 2nd Caçadores served in Lecor's own brigade, and fought at Vitoria in 1813, the battle that drove the French from Spain. Wellington came to rate the Caçadores among the best light troops in his army. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

GUARD.name: 3rd Caçadores
GUARD.bio: The 3rd Caçadores served in the famous Light Division alongside the 95th Rifles, among the finest light troops in Wellington's army. At Bussaco in 1810 the Light Division waited in hiding on the ridge until the French columns were almost upon them, then rose and drove them back down the slope. The Portuguese light infantry fought beside the British riflemen through the rest of the war. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: 1st Line Regiment (Lisbon)
INFANTRY.bio: The 1st Line Regiment was one of Lisbon's regiments and fought in Pack's Portuguese brigade at Bussaco in September 1810, the first great battle in which Beresford's retrained Portuguese stood beside the British in Wellington's line. Their steadiness on the ridge that day showed that the reforms had worked. Portuguese line infantry wore dark blue with regimental facings. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: 16th Line Regiment
INFANTRY.bio: The 16th Line Regiment fought alongside the 1st Line in Pack's brigade at Bussaco in 1810, where Masséna's columns broke against the Allied line on the ridge. The Portuguese brigades were mixed into British divisions, and by the end of the war a large share of Wellington's infantry was Portuguese. The 16th served on through the campaigns that followed. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: 7th Line Regiment (Setúbal)
INFANTRY.bio: The 7th Line Regiment, recruited around Setúbal, served in Lecor's brigade during the later Peninsular campaigns. It marched with Wellington's army through Spain and into France in 1813 and 1814. Portuguese regiments like the 7th made up a large part of the army that ended the war on French soil. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: 19th Line Regiment (Cascais)
INFANTRY.bio: The 19th Line Regiment, from Cascais near Lisbon, fought in Lecor's brigade at Vitoria in June 1813, when Wellington's army broke the French in Spain and captured King Joseph's baggage train.
