Through 1813 and 1814 Portuguese line regiments like the 19th fought in the Pyrenees and on into southern France, earning Wellington's praise as the fighting cocks of his army. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: 23rd Line Regiment (Almeida)
INFANTRY.bio: The 23rd Line Regiment was Carlos Frederico Lecor's first command as a colonel, in 1808, at the start of the war against the French. Lecor went on to command brigades and then a division in Wellington's army. Years later, after leading Portuguese veterans to Brazil, he died in Rio de Janeiro as a Marshal of the Brazilian Army. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: Royal Volunteers of the Prince
INFANTRY.bio: The Divisão de Voluntários Reais do Príncipe was formed in 1815 on the orders of the Prince Regent, João, from some 5,000 men, mostly veterans of the Peninsular War. Under Lecor it landed at Rio de Janeiro on 30 March 1816 and then marched south, occupying Montevideo in January 1817 and carrying Portugal's Brazilian frontier to the River Plate. Its veterans later held Montevideo as the last Portuguese stronghold in South America after Brazil declared independence. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

HEAVY_CAV.name: 1st Cavalry (Alcântara)
HEAVY_CAV.bio: The 1st Cavalry Regiment, Alcântara, was the senior regiment of the Portuguese cavalry. Portugal's horsemen were rebuilt under Beresford alongside the infantry, though horses were always scarce after the French invasions. The Portuguese cavalry served in brigades with the British dragoons through the later campaigns of the war. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

HEAVY_CAV.name: 4th Cavalry (Mecklenburg)
HEAVY_CAV.bio: The 4th Cavalry Regiment carried the name of its princely colonel-proprietor, a member of the house of Mecklenburg, in the old European fashion. Like the rest of Portugal's mounted arm it was reorganised under Beresford after 1809 and served with Wellington's army. Portuguese cavalry fought in support of the Allied army in the Peninsula through to 1814. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

LIGHT_CAV.name: 6th Cavalry (Bragança)
LIGHT_CAV.bio: The 6th Cavalry Regiment took the name of Bragança, the royal house of Portugal whose prince regent had sailed for Brazil in 1807 and ruled the empire from Rio de Janeiro. Raised in the north of the country, it served as light horse with the Allied army. Its riders scouted and screened for the infantry through the campaigns that drove the French out of Portugal. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

LIGHT_CAV.name: 8th Cavalry (Elvas)
LIGHT_CAV.bio: The 8th Cavalry Regiment was named after Elvas, the great frontier fortress facing Spanish Badajoz across the border. Raised in the Alentejo, the regiment served with the Allied cavalry through the years of fighting along the Portuguese frontier, where Wellington's army besieged Badajoz and Ciudad Rodrigo. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

ARTILLERY.name: Battery of da Cunha Preto
ARTILLERY.bio: The Portuguese Royal Artillery was reorganised under Beresford and served alongside the British and King's German Legion batteries in Wellington's army. Captain da Cunha Preto's battery was one of the Portuguese batteries in action at Bussaco in 1810, firing down from the ridge on Masséna's columns as they toiled up the slope. If brigaded entirely with Cavalry, fights as Horse Artillery at Cavalry speed, except when crossing a ploughed field.

ARTILLERY.name: Battery of Freira
ARTILLERY.bio: Freira's battery was the second of the Portuguese batteries engaged at Bussaco in September 1810, where the Allied army beat off Masséna's assaults on the ridge. The Portuguese gunners proved themselves the equal of their British comrades, and the artillery served on with Wellington through the campaigns of 1811 to 1814. If brigaded entirely with Cavalry, fights as Horse Artillery at Cavalry speed, except when crossing a ploughed field.

BRIGADIER.name: Poniatowski
BRIGADIER.bio: Prince Józef Poniatowski, nephew of the last King of Poland, became Minister of War of the Duchy of Warsaw and the commander of its army. In 1809 he held an Austrian force twice his size to a standstill at Raszyn, and in 1812 he led the all-Polish V Corps, 36,000 strong, at Smolensk and Borodino. Made a Marshal of the Empire at Leipzig on 16 October 1813, he was cut off three days later when the Elster bridge was blown, led a last charge, and drowned trying to swim the river after being wounded four times. Holds one Leadership Roll for the match, a single guaranteed Rally save for a unit under his command.

BRIGADIER.name: Dąbrowski
BRIGADIER.bio: Jan Henryk Dąbrowski founded the Polish Legions in Italy in 1797, gathering exiled Poles to fight for France in the hope of restoring their country. The song written for his legionnaires, with its promise that Poland has not yet perished, became the Polish national anthem. He raised the uprising of 1806 that brought Polish troops back to their homeland alongside Napoleon, and commanded a division in the Russian campaign of 1812. Holds one Leadership Roll for the match, a single guaranteed Rally save for a unit under his command.

BRIGADIER.name: Krasiński
BRIGADIER.bio: Wincenty Krasiński commanded the 1st Polish Light Horse Regiment of the Imperial Guard from its formation in 1807 until Napoleon's first abdication in 1814. Under him the regiment became one of the most celebrated cavalry units in Europe, riding as part of Napoleon's personal escort from Spain to Russia and on into France. Its officers went on to command so widely that the regiment was called a school for generals. Holds one Leadership Roll for the match, a single guaranteed Rally save for a unit under his command.

GUARD.name: 1st Vistula Legion Infantry
GUARD.bio: The Vistula Legion grew out of the Poles serving in Italy and was renamed in 1808, with the same status as French line units. Its veteran regiments were sent into Spain, where they fought through both terrible sieges of Zaragoza in 1808 and 1809, street by street and house by house. Withdrawn for the invasion of Russia, the legion fought at Smolensk and Borodino and its survivors were still in the line at Leipzig. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

GUARD.name: 2nd Vistula Legion Infantry
GUARD.bio: The 2nd Regiment of the Vistula Legion marched into Spain in June 1808 and became part of the long and savage campaign there, fighting alongside the French at the sieges of Zaragoza. Hardened by years of war against Spanish regulars and guerrillas alike, the legion's men were among the most experienced soldiers Poland put in the field. In 1812 each regiment of the legion was given its own small battery of two light guns for the march on Moscow. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: 1st Polish Infantry Regiment
INFANTRY.bio: The 1st Infantry Regiment of the Army of the Duchy of Warsaw was raised in 1806 and served until the Duchy's army was reorganised in 1814. It fought at Raszyn and at Praga in 1809 as Poniatowski defended the Duchy against the Austrians, and its colours bore the white silk inscription Pułk Pierwszy Piechoty above the eagle. It marched into Russia in 1812 and fought on to the Battle of Leipzig. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: 3rd Polish Infantry Regiment
INFANTRY.bio: The 3rd Infantry Regiment took its name by order of Poniatowski as Minister of War in June 1807, and was garrisoned in Warsaw. In 1809 it fought at Raszyn, then at Zamość and Sandomierz as the Poles carried the war into Austrian Galicia. By the end of that year it numbered more than 2,600 men. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: 8th Polish Infantry Regiment
INFANTRY.bio: The 8th Infantry Regiment began as the 4th Regiment of the Kalisz Legion and was commanded by the poet Cyprian Godebski. At Raszyn in April 1809 Godebski was killed leading the regiment's 1st Battalion into the attack, a death later painted by January Suchodolski. The regiment went on to fight at Smolensk and Borodino in 1812. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: 2nd Polish Infantry Regiment
INFANTRY.bio: The 2nd Infantry Regiment was one of the line regiments raised for the new Polish army during the rising of 1806 and 1807, as Poles flocked to Napoleon's cause after the fall of Prussia. Like the rest of the Duchy's infantry it was organised, armed and drilled on the French model, in three battalions of six companies. It served through the defence of the Duchy in 1809 and the campaigns that followed. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: 3rd Vistula Legion Infantry
INFANTRY.bio: The 3rd Regiment of the Vistula Legion entered Spain with the 2nd in June 1808 and spent the following years in the hard fighting of the Peninsula. Brought back for the Russian campaign in 1812, it was ordered to recruit a third battalion, which did not catch up with the regiment until the retreat from Moscow was well under way. Its survivors were merged into a single Vistula Regiment in 1813. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: 4th Vistula Legion Infantry
INFANTRY.bio: The 4th Regiment of the Vistula Legion was born of the short-lived Second Vistula Legion, which Napoleon ordered raised from prisoners taken from the Austrians in 1809. When that legion failed to recruit up to strength it was disbanded in February 1810, and its men were folded into the original legion as its 4th Regiment. It served with the legion through the invasion of Russia. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

HEAVY_CAV.name: 1st Polish Light Horse of the Guard
HEAVY_CAV.bio: The 1er Régiment de Chevau-légers Polonais de la Garde Impériale was raised in 1807 and served as part of Napoleon's escort. At Somosierra in November 1808 a single squadron of about 125 men under Jan Kozietulski charged up a narrow mountain road against four Spanish batteries, sabres drawn, and took them in a charge said to have lasted seven minutes, opening the road to Madrid. Afterwards the regiment took up the lance and fought in every campaign to 1815. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

HEAVY_CAV.name: 14th Polish Cuirassiers
HEAVY_CAV.bio: The 14th Cuirassier Regiment was the Duchy of Warsaw's heavy cavalry, armoured horsemen raised for the invasion of Russia in 1812. At Borodino it rode in the 7th Heavy Cavalry Division of Latour-Maubourg's IV Cavalry Corps, brigaded with Saxon and Westphalian cuirassiers. That division took part in the great cavalry assault on the Russian centre around the Raevsky Redoubt. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

LIGHT_CAV.name: 1st Vistula Lancers
LIGHT_CAV.bio: The 1st Lancer Regiment of the Vistula Legion had to prove the worth of the lance to a sceptical Napoleon in 1808, and proved it beyond doubt at Albuera on 16 May 1811. Bursting out of a rainstorm onto the flank and rear of Colborne's British brigade, the lancers destroyed three of its four battalions, taking prisoners, guns and colours in one of the most devastating cavalry charges of the Peninsular War. In 1811 the regiment passed into the French line as the 7th Chevau-légers Lanciers. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

LIGHT_CAV.name: Krakus Horse
LIGHT_CAV.bio: The Krakus were light horsemen raised from the peasants of the Kraków region, riding small, hardy horses and armed with lances in the manner of Cossacks. Poniatowski brought them into his corps for the 1813 campaign in Germany, where they served as scouts and skirmishers against the Russian Cossacks they so closely resembled. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

ARTILLERY.name: Duchy of Warsaw Foot Artillery
ARTILLERY.bio: The foot artillery of the Duchy of Warsaw was built on the French model, with French-style guns, drill and organisation, and served with Poniatowski's V Corps in 1812. At Borodino the Polish guns supported the attacks on Utitsa and its mound on the far right of the French line. In 1813 they fought through the campaign in Saxony to the final battle at Leipzig. If brigaded entirely with Cavalry, fights as Horse Artillery at Cavalry speed, except when crossing a ploughed field.

ARTILLERY.name: Polish Horse Artillery
ARTILLERY.bio: The Polish horse artillery rode with the Duchy's lancers, every gunner mounted so the guns could keep pace with the cavalry. At Borodino two Polish horse batteries supported the three regiments of Polish uhlans in the 4th Light Cavalry Division of Latour-Maubourg's corps. They served on with the cavalry through the retreat and the campaign of 1813. If brigaded entirely with Cavalry, fights as Horse Artillery at Cavalry speed, except when crossing a ploughed field.

BRIGADIER.name: Eugène de Beauharnais
BRIGADIER.bio: Eugène de Beauharnais, Napoleon's stepson, ruled the Kingdom of Italy as Viceroy and commanded its army through the wars of 1809 to 1814. In Russia he led the IV Corps, largely Italian, and at Maloyaroslavets in October 1812 threw in his Italian division to win a town that changed hands eight times in a day. When Murat abandoned the shattered Grande Armée on the retreat, it was Eugène who took command of what was left of it. Holds one Leadership Roll for the match, a single guaranteed Rally save for a unit under his command.

BRIGADIER.name: Pino
BRIGADIER.bio: Domenico Pino of Milan was Minister of War of the Kingdom of Italy and its best-known fighting general. He led Italian divisions in Prussia in 1807 and in Spain from 1808 to 1810, and in 1812 commanded the 15th (Italian) Division of Eugène's IV Corps. At Maloyaroslavets his division, in action for the first time that campaign, was thrown into the burning town to drive the Russians out; his brother Giacomo was killed in the fighting. Holds one Leadership Roll for the match, a single guaranteed Rally save for a unit under his command.

BRIGADIER.name: Guglielmo Pepe
BRIGADIER.bio: Guglielmo Pepe was a Calabrian officer who served the French-ruled Kingdom of Naples under Joseph Bonaparte and then Murat, fighting in the Peninsula with the Neapolitan contingent. He rose to general in Murat's army and fought in the Neapolitan War of 1815, when Murat marched north to make himself master of Italy and was beaten by the Austrians at Tolentino. A lifelong patriot, Pepe later led the Neapolitan revolution of 1820. Holds one Leadership Roll for the match, a single guaranteed Rally save for a unit under his command.

GUARD.name: Italian Guard Grenadiers
GUARD.bio: The Granatieri of the Italian Royal Guard were the senior infantry of the Kingdom of Italy, modelled closely on Napoleon's Imperial Guard and wearing bearskins and the green and white of the Italian kingdom. The Royal Guard marched into Russia with Eugène's IV Corps in 1812. At Maloyaroslavets it was said to have displayed qualities that entitled it evermore to rank among the bravest troops of Europe, and the battle is still remembered in Italy as the Battle of the Italians. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

GUARD.name: Italian Guard Velites
GUARD.bio: The Veliti Reali of the Italian Royal Guard were picked young men who served in the Guard and trained there as future officers, in imitation of the French Guard's vélites. They fought alongside the Guard grenadiers through the campaigns of the Kingdom of Italy, from Austria in 1809 to Russia in 1812. Few of the Italian Guard returned from the retreat from Moscow. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: 1st Italian Light Infantry
INFANTRY.bio: The 1st Light Infantry Regiment was one of the light regiments of the Army of the Kingdom of Italy, organised on the French model with chasseurs and voltigeur companies trained to skirmish ahead of the line. Italian light infantry served with Eugène in the war against Austria in 1809 and with the IV Corps in Russia in 1812. Napoleon came to regard his Italian troops as among the most dependable of his allies. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: 2nd Italian Line Infantry
INFANTRY.bio: The 2nd Line Infantry Regiment belonged to the army of the Kingdom of Italy, recruited by conscription across Lombardy, Venetia and the Romagna and dressed in white coats with distinguishing facings. Italian line regiments served in Spain under Pino and others from 1808, where they fought through the long sieges and counter-guerrilla war in Catalonia. In 1812 Italian line infantry marched into Russia with the IV Corps. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: 3rd Italian Line Infantry
INFANTRY.bio: The 3rd Line Infantry Regiment of the Kingdom of Italy served through the Empire's wars from Austria to Russia. In the campaign of 1812 the Italian infantry of the IV Corps fought at Maloyaroslavets, where the corps took the town against Dokhturov's and Raevsky's Russians. In 1813 and 1814 the regiment fought with Eugène in the defence of northern Italy against the Austrians. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: Dalmatian Regiment
INFANTRY.bio: The Royal Dalmatian Regiment was raised from the Adriatic coast of Dalmatia after it passed to the Kingdom of Italy, drawing on a coastal people with a long tradition of soldiering for Venice. Its men served in the Italian army's campaigns, including the invasion of Russia in 1812. Dalmatians were valued as tough, hardy infantry, well used to fighting in difficult country. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: Neapolitan Guard Velites
INFANTRY.bio: The Velites of the Neapolitan Royal Guard formed part of the Guard Division that Joachim Murat led north in 1815, when he broke with the Allies and marched to unite Italy under his own crown. At Tolentino in May 1815 the Guard Division descended from Monte Milone against the Austrian left flank, but the attack failed and Murat's army was destroyed. Two Velite regiments, each about a thousand men, stood in the line that day. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

INFANTRY.name: Neapolitan 10th Line
INFANTRY.bio: The 10th Line Infantry Regiment belonged to the army that Murat built in the Kingdom of Naples on French lines after 1808. Neapolitan troops served Napoleon in Spain and in Germany, and in 1815 the line regiments marched north with Murat's 40,000 men for the Neapolitan War against Austria. At Tolentino the 10th, 11th and 12th Line fought together as a combined force of about 1,100 men. Can stack with another Infantry unit to form an Attack Column, and may Lay Ambush if holding an unwatched wood instead of moving.

HEAVY_CAV.name: Dragoni Napoleone
HEAVY_CAV.bio: The Dragoni Napoleone, the Napoleon Dragoons, were one of the two dragoon regiments of the Kingdom of Italy, named in honour of its king, the Emperor himself. As early as 1807 they served at the siege of Colberg on the Baltic, alongside Polish and Württemberg troops in the force sent against the Prussian fortress. They went on to fight in Spain and with Eugène in Russia in 1812. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

HEAVY_CAV.name: Dragoni della Regina
HEAVY_CAV.bio: The Dragoni della Regina, the Queen's Dragoons, were the second dragoon regiment of the Kingdom of Italy, named in honour of the Empress Joséphine. With the Napoleon Dragoons they took part in the siege of Colberg in 1807, and later served in Spain and in the campaigns of 1809 and 1812. The Italian dragoons were considered good heavy cavalry, mounted on strong horses from the plains of Lombardy. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

LIGHT_CAV.name: Neapolitan Guard Hussars
LIGHT_CAV.bio: The Hussars of the Neapolitan Royal Guard were the showpiece of Murat's cavalry, raised by a king who had made his name as the most flamboyant cavalryman in Europe and dressed his own Guard accordingly. At Tolentino in 1815 they rode with the Guard cavalry, some 426 men on 556 horses. Murat's love of display was matched by real courage, and his Guard horsemen fought hard in the battle that cost him his throne. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

LIGHT_CAV.name: Neapolitan Guard Lancers
LIGHT_CAV.bio: The Lancers of the Neapolitan Royal Guard were one of four Guard cavalry units, alongside hussars, mounted chasseurs and chevau-légers, that Murat took north in the Neapolitan War of 1815. Around 300 strong at Tolentino, they were armed with the lance on the Polish model then fashionable across the French-allied armies. They shared the defeat that ended Murat's reign and, within months, his life. Can declare a Charge across open ground, winning any tie on the first round of the resulting fight.

ARTILLERY.name: Italian Guard Horse Artillery
ARTILLERY.bio: The Horse Artillery of the Italian Royal Guard supported the Guard cavalry and the reserves of Eugène's army, every gunner mounted so the guns could gallop into action. Trained to French standards, the Italian artillery was among the best arms of the Kingdom's army. It served with the IV Corps in Russia in 1812 and in the defence of Italy in 1813 and 1814. If brigaded entirely with Cavalry, fights as Horse Artillery at Cavalry speed, except when crossing a ploughed field.

ARTILLERY.name: Neapolitan Foot Artillery
ARTILLERY.bio: The foot artillery of the Kingdom of Naples was reorganised on French lines after 1806, first under Joseph Bonaparte and then under Murat. In 1815 Murat took fifty-six guns north for the Neapolitan War. The Neapolitan gunners fought at Tolentino and in the string of rearguard actions that followed the defeat. If brigaded entirely with Cavalry, fights as Horse Artillery at Cavalry speed, except when crossing a ploughed field.
